sections.html:
New Rochelle homeowners deal with four separate deadlines a year, because four taxing bodies (the city, Westchester County, the schools and the public library) each bill on their own calendar. The City Tax Department collects all four. A payment that arrives after the due month ends picks up interest and penalties. The city's Property Tax Schedule has the current list.

Bills collected by the New Rochelle Tax Department
BillDue on or beforePeriod it covers
City taxJanuary 31January 1 to December 31
County taxJune 30January 1 to December 31
School and library, first halfSeptember 30July 1 to December 31
School and library, second halfMarch 31January 1 to June 30

The school and library year runs July to June, while the city and county bills follow the calendar year. A closing date in the middle of the year lands in a different slice of each bill, so ask the closing attorney or title company to adjust all four separately.

sections.h2: Where to pay and who to call
sections.html:
The City of New Rochelle Tax Department sends the bills and takes the payments for the city, Westchester County, the New Rochelle City School District and the New Rochelle Public Library. Assessments come from a different office, the Bureau of Assessments inside the Finance Department, which prepares the roll that every one of those bills is built on.

  • Assessor's Office: 515 North Avenue, New Rochelle, NY 10801, weekdays 8:30 am to 4:30 pm, telephone (914) 654-2052.
  • Online: the city's payment portal takes cards and e-checks. Convenience fees apply.
  • In person: the Tax Office is on the ground floor of City Hall at the same North Avenue address.
  • By mail: make the check payable to Tax Collector New Rochelle and write the block and lot number on it. The city advises against paying through personal online banking.
  • Direct debit: the city can draw payments automatically from a checking or money market account once you return its authorization form.

Two web tools show parcel data. CitySquared offers mapping, parcel basics and building permit information, and the SDG Property Information portal adds photos and tax history. For the tax rate on your own parcel, ask the Tax Department.

sections.h2: Owning and selling a house in New Rochelle
sections.html:
New Rochelle is a Long Island Sound city of 85,864 people (July 2025 estimate, up 7.7 percent from 2020) with 31,684 households. About 53.7 percent of housing units are owner-occupied, and a typical owned home is valued at $702,500, with median gross rent at $1,917. Nicknamed the "City of Homes," it has Metro-North service downtown.

Water is part of life here. The city keeps a page for owners with chronic flooding. If a home is damaged enough to lower its value and the repairs are not done by December 1, the owner can contact the assessor in April to arrange an inspection.

The year turns on December 1, the taxable status date. Every property is assessed on its condition that day, and December 1 is also the deadline for filing exemption applications with the Assessor's Office, in person or by mail to 515 North Avenue.

  • December 1: taxable status date and exemption deadline.
  • February 1: the tentative assessment roll is published.
  • Third Tuesday in February: Grievance Day.
  • April 1: the final assessment roll. A changed assessment shows up in the billing cycle that begins September 1.

The city has not run a citywide reassessment since 1956, so values on the roll rarely track the sale prices you see around town. Renovations are the exception. Work finished in a given year is reviewed as of that year's December 1, and any new figure appears on the next February roll. If you plan a kitchen or an addition before listing, you can ask the City Appraiser for an estimate of the effect on your assessment.

sections.h2: How do I file a grievance on my New Rochelle assessment?
sections.html:
File Form RP-524 with the Assessor's Office between February 1 and the third Tuesday in February. Applications outside that window cannot be accepted, as the city's grievance page spells out.

  • Look at your tentative roll entry on or after February 1. It shows the assessed value and the assessor's estimate of market value.
  • Gather at least three recent arm's length sales of similar homes close by, matched on size, style, age, condition and lot.
  • Submit the original application in person or by mail. Email and fax copies are refused.
  • File one application for each parcel if you own more than one or your property spans several lots.
  • Ask the Assessor's Office for a hearing time with the Board of Assessment Review after the form is in.

The board is made up of residents appointed by the City Council, and no assessor staff sit on it. If your assessment is fair but the bill still feels heavy, the assessor cannot help, since tax rates are set by the council, the school district and the county legislature. After the grievance stage, most homeowners can go on to Small Claims Assessment Review, but New York requires the local grievance first.

A new owner who applies for STAR receives it as a check or direct deposit from the state. You register with New York State at tax.ny.gov/star, and the credit requires a primary residence and combined income of all owners and spouses of $500,000 or less.

The older Basic STAR exemption stays in place for people who applied before May 1, 2015, with a combined income under $250,000, and its savings have been capped since 2019. Enhanced STAR is for owners 65 or older within the state income limit, and the state now moves eligible owners over without a new application. Other exemptions are filed with the New Rochelle assessor by December 1.

When you sell, close your STAR registration. Your buyer registers as the new owner of the home.

Open balances get settled as part of the sale, so start by asking the Tax Department for a statement of every unpaid bill on the parcel. Check the city's fee lists as well. Unpaid false alarm charges move onto the next city tax bill after September 30, and restored to roll, sidewalk repair and property maintenance charges move over after December 1.

The deed itself is recorded with the Westchester County Clerk, not at City Hall. The assessor can't change ownership records at the city level and points owners to an attorney, who files the papers with the county clerk.

If you are behind on taxes, tell your closing attorney or title company early so the payoff figures are ready before the closing date. A buyer paying cash still needs those figures, and having them in hand before you sign a contract keeps the closing date from slipping. Bring the latest bills for all four taxing bodies, any fee notices, and the deed information to your first meeting with the attorney.

faqs.q: Which office handles New Rochelle assessment questions?
faqs.a: The Assessor's Office at 515 North Avenue, reachable at (914) 654-2052 on weekdays. It answers questions about assessed value, exemptions and grievance forms but has no say over the tax rate.

faqs.q: When is Grievance Day in New Rochelle?
faqs.a: It falls on the third Tuesday in February. Applications can be filed from February 1 through that Tuesday, and the tentative roll comes out on February 1.

faqs.q: Can I pay a New Rochelle tax bill with a credit card?
faqs.a: Yes, through the city's online payment portal, which also takes e-checks. Convenience fees apply. You can also pay at the City Hall Tax Office, by mail or by direct debit.

faqs.q: Is the New Rochelle school tax due once a year?
faqs.a: No. It is split into two halves, due on or before September 30 and March 31. The library bill rides along with the school bill.

faqs.q: Who pays the March school installment if I sell in the winter?
faqs.a: That depends on your contract and the closing adjustments. The March bill covers January through June, so ask your attorney how the closing statement will divide it.
